articles.title: FlatOut 4: Total Insanity VR Leaves PC VR Early Access Today With New Features & A New Price
articles.summary: FlatOut 4: Total Insanity VR exits Early Access with new features, more vehicles, more maps, and a new price of $29.99.
articles.text: FlatOut 4: Total Insanity VR Leaves PC VR Early Access Today With New Features & A New Price Carnage-fueled racer FlatOut 4: Total Insanity VR has gone to its 1.0 full release, adding multiple new features and a price increase to $29.99. Version 1.0 adds multiple new features and content, including one that Flat2VR Studios' Elliott Tate teased to me in our interview earlier this year: first-person vehicle ejections . Anyone willing to test their VR sea legs in Stunt mode or crashes in races (like me) is free to do so with a first-person camera instead of the Early Access method that shifted to third person view in such cases. Here's a list of the new additions: An overhaul to the multiplayer system redesigns the lobbies to be faster to get into a race. You can also now join active sessions, fill out your lobbies with AI racers and spectator functions including passenger ride-alongs. AI settings to tweak the behavior of non-human opponents. The opponent AI has also been improved overall. Support for bHaptics, motion rigs, and additional steering wheels. New options for FlatOut 2 physics. New vehicles, including multiple cars and a motorcycle. Updated UI and menu interactions, bug fixes, and performance optimizations. The new price now matches the original FlatOut 4's cost. The VR port was originally $19.99 in Early Access. Price increases out of Early Access are not uncommon in gaming. articles.title: Switch 2 security takes a hit as hackers unlock homebrew access
articles.summary: "Userland" exploit relies on integer overflow found in "SmileBasic" interpreter.
articles.text: Switch 2 security takes a hit as hackers unlock homebrew access A security researcher has demonstrated a software-only partial jailbreak of the Switch 2, gaining "userland" access that he says "lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO." The hack relies on the original Switch version of SmileBasic 4 , the latest in a long-running series of programming environments and interpreters that run on Nintendo hardware. The so-called "tethered" hack also requires access to a macOS or Linux PC on the same network to run a node.js package that helps enable privileged system access. Researcher Sammy Hajhamid writes that he used OpenAI's Codex to poke at SmileBasic's language interpreter, using a custom harness that could send USB commands to the system and view results via HDMI (as well as power cycling via a Bluetooth light switch flipping device). After "substantial effort for ~2 weeks," that harness discovered a 32-bit integer overflow that occurs when removing items from an array in SmileBasic. That error gives access to an array pointer, which in turn allows read-and-write access to portions of system memory. Read full article Comments

Don't forget about your Nintendo DS just yet, as one of the most famous and revered survival horrors of all time is making its way to Ninty's pride and joy. A team of modders are working to bring Resident Evil 2 to the DS with dual-screen support in a new homebrew project, 'Resident Evil 2: Deadly Science'. Of course, 'Resident Evil: Deadly Science' already exists for the DS and is an enhanced version of the original PS1 game. It came to the DS as part of the 10th anniversary celebrations for the series and released in all territories throughout 2006. And of course, Deadly Science has the initials 'DS', which is a nice little touch. The project uses REA (Reverse Engineer Anything) and Claude Code, with a team of human devs sifting through the code and making sure things work. Admittedly, the team behind the project have said that it's still rough and that there's still a way to go, but so far the first two cutscenes are working properly, as well as the 'core loop' of picking up and combining items, taking down zombies, and running out of health to the point where you K.O. Music and sound effects are all working too. articles.title: AMD brings official Ryzen overclocking to Linux with AOD driver support
articles.summary: New driver enablement work from AMD brings full platform-level tuning control to Ryzen systems running Linux, finally.
articles.text: AMD brings official Ryzen overclocking to Linux with AOD driver support While Windows overclockers have spent years lazily sliding UI controls to adjust frequency curves and tweak voltages inside Ryzen Master, Linux users have largely had to treat their CPU tuning like an archaeological dig into the opaque veil of UEFI/BIOS firmware. Well, rejoice, Linux users, as AMD has officially published a fresh set of patches for the Linux kernel introducing AOD (AMD Overclocking Driver) support for Ryzen processors, Phoronix reports. Instead of forcing developers to reverse-engineer closed-source firmware hooks or rely on messy, machine-specific ACPI workarounds, this new kernel driver is a direct pipeline to AMD's platform adjustments. By exposing core tuning capabilities straight through the standard sysfs interface, AMD is laying down an official, upstreamed foundation for software-level CPU management. Right out of the gate, the driver handles platform-level SMT toggling, memory clock visibility, and power tunables. That's right: you can now toggle Simultaneous Multithreading (SMT) dynamically through this driver interface. That works through the CPU hotplugging mechanism and acts as a clean alternative to passing the old 'nosmt' boot parameter to the kernel. The new driver also allows real-time monitoring of memory clocks, and initial power controls are being wired up, too. articles.text: ‘Gears of War: E-Day’ PC VR Mod is Coming with Support for Full Campaign Gears of War: E-Day (2026) has only been out for a little over two weeks now, and there's already a PC VR mod in the works to get you up close and personal with the Locust Horde. A free mod being created by ‘ rockonthehill ‘ is set to bring full VR support for the entire campaign. Items already crossed off the list include full stereo rendering, full-body IK, manual reloads, manual weapon switching, two-handed aiming, the ability to fight from cover, and take on the gunner position when in the King Raven. Check out the video below to see it in action: Notably, the mod is also only intended for the single-player campaign right now, and not online coop, rockonthehill says. And the mod is admittedly still an early work in progress as well, so there's no telling when we'll see its GitHub repo, which is likely be a fork of Praydog's UEVR mod for Unreal Engine games. Still, there is active development going on, so all signs point to imminent release. Future updates are said to include Lancer chainsaw (no canned animations), physical melee, colliders for hands and weapons, and a real working scope for Longshot. We'll get to see all of that in its next feature drop video soon, rockonthehill says, noting the mod will be free when it releases at some point in the future. The new levels are played from the viewpoint of the COI (Covert Operations Initiative), the antagonist organization of the game. Support Group features COI agents who managed to survive encounters with the game's protagonist, retired agent Alphonse Harding. The agents recount their overexaggerated stories of Harding's seemingly unreal abilities as you play the scenarios out in real time. This same story expansion was added to the original game in 2024. articles.text: Let's reverse-engineer how someone reverse-engineered a secret hiding in F-Zero GX for 23 years Hello again! We're back, and yet another fortnight has passed without me losing the last shreds of my sanity while trying to distinguish between the shoddily assembled AI rubbish piling up in every corner of this little hobby and the good stuff that I delight in sharing with you all. Check back in two weeks' time for another exciting update! Oh, right: There's still a newsletter to do. Well despite being weighed down by said winnowing process, I've cobbled together some cool stuff for you, including a bit of insight into how someone found a secret hiding inside one of the best games ever made and a quick check-in on some of the emulation hardware we'll be playing our games on this time next year. It's not even Android stuff! As is often the case, though, the best stuff may be down in the Translation Station, at least if you're a fan of Puyo Puyo or strange, Bionic Commando-adjacent PS2 action games ( boy, am I!!). They're blessedly AI-free, and there are more people out there still fighting the good fight. Just wait for Mermanoid and Schrodinger no Neko from some crack teams! The original flatscreen version of Titanfall 2 leveraged an innovative combination of free-flowing movement, precision shooting mechanics, and mech-based combat to make you feel like the most powerful force on the battlefield. While certain aspects of Titanfall 2 are more effective in VR, others get lost in translation. In the end, though there are frequent moments throughout its campaign that remind you the original game was not made with VR in mind, the Titanfall 2 VR Mod is still one of the best VR mods I’ve ever played. articles.title: Long-lost horror gaming cult classic P.T. gets a much-needed PC port
articles.summary: Kojima's discontinued "playable trailer" is no longer stuck on a few aging PS4 hard drives.
articles.text: Long-lost horror gaming cult classic P.T. gets a much-needed PC port For over a decade now, the only "official" way to play Hideo Kojima's cult classic, P.T. —the long-discontinued "playable trailer" for Kojima's canceled "Silent Hills" project —has been via one of the increasingly rare PlayStation 4s that previously downloaded a copy during its monthslong availability window. Now, though, one coder is helping to preserve the game with a porting tool that builds a playable x86 PC executable from the original PS4 files. Coder Lorean Xavier said he was inspired to work on the "P.T. for PC" project "because P.T. deserved to keep existing somewhere other than on consoles that still have it installed." The open source porting effort rebuilds the P.T. engine in C++ and Vulkan, using the original files from the PS4 game to re-create "every level, model, texture, sound, script and cutscene," according to its GitHub listing. That means players without their own legitimate decrypted copy of the original P.T. will have to track one down in order to generate a playable PC version. The reliance on real P.T. files makes this port more authentic than previous hobbyist efforts to re-create the look and feel of P.T. for a PC audience. articles.text: Titanfall 2's VR Mod Is Stellar, And Its Installer Is The Best Thing About It CircuitLord's turnkey solution to one of VR modding's many friction points feels like a bigger step forward than yet another example of a great VR mod for an already great game. Getting the immediate question out of the way, yes, the Titanfall 2 VR mod is as great as advertised. Rather than a barely-performant, deeply flawed, subpar "early version" mod that wouldn't qualify for early access status if it were an actual game, like many of the vibe coded VR mods that popped up over the summer (yes, I played several of them), the TF2 mod feels like a finished product out of the gate. We will have another article soon from a writer who had never played Titanfall 2 prior to the mod that gets into what makes it great. Having previously played the game myself, I cannot offer that perspective. 0:00 / 0:50 1× Titanfall 2 VR mod gameplay captured by UploadVR In spite of my enthusiasm for VR as a medium, I despise extensive tinkering and troubleshooting in any form. After a long workday and any needed household/family duties, when I put on a headset and press play for a game, I want it to just work. VR mods have always actively worked against that innate desire for a turnkey implementation. articles.text: PS5 emulation has gotten an AI turbocharge. So what now? Hello one, hello all! We're back, and somehow — I'm just getting reports of this now — it's already spooky season ? How the hell did that happen, man. Wasn't I just writing about Screaming Mad George's pinball nightmare a few months ago? Did spending the first three weeks of September in Asia where it was like 90 degrees and wetter than the inside of a mouth throw off my seasonal radar? Quite possibly . But here we are barreling towards the end of the year nonetheless. I've fallen woefully behind in my optimistic plan to play a bunch of fan translations this year, though there's still some time left before I declare that plan a failure! I'm hoping to sneak in Cabal Translations' London Seirei Tanteidan by year's end, and am greatly looking forward to Hilltop's "Fan Translation Direct" which aims to celebrate human-made patches whenever it comes together. On that subject: You may have seen on social media that longtime translator Eien Ni Hen tragically passed away in recent weeks. I didn't know her personally, and wish I'd had a chance to interview her about her decades of selfless work in bringing Japanese games to English audiences. articles.title: Introducing Warp Point, a Web 1.0 gaming blog directory built for 2026
articles.summary: It's a webring! And a website!
articles.text: Introducing Warp Point, a Web 1.0 gaming blog directory built for 2026 In January 2024, just a few weeks after I decided to ditch Substack over its unwillingness to kick Nazis off its platform, I jotted down this half-formed thought in a scratch pad: What if we banded together and created a gaming webring? Pretend there's a bunch of inspirational stuff here. Togetherness is the path forward! Down with big tech! Up with open source! More thoughtful words! At the time, I didn't have the bandwidth to turn this small pile of notes, which included another header — "Bringing back 88x31 buttons" — into reality. But I kept thinking about it throughout 2024. And 2025. And in 2026, I stopped thinking about it and started doing it. Meet Warp Point , a throwback to the days of directories and webrings, built solely for independent games writing. Warp Point A curated list of gaming blogs that support RSS. Inspired by the more communal Web 1.0 era and one of the best sites on the internet, Ooh.directory , Warp Point is built around simple technologies like RSS with a simple premise: Helping writers connect with people who love to read about games, and with other people who love to write about them. There are no algorithms. No AI summaries. No paid promo slots or accounts meant to keep you on the site. We want you to leave — by browsing through the list of independent bloggers and essayists and newsletter writers and archivists, finding one that interests you, and clicking on it. Hopefully
